all_opposition.description: The 500 bighas granted to the Deoshis were included in the earlier 5,800-bigha grant to the Singhs. The overlapping grants explain the ensuing title suit.
The earlier title-and-possession dispute was resolved by a compromise decree rather than by the initial unconditional establishment of one side's entitlement.
The declaration and hereditary-tenancy provisions in the compromise are subject to its express payment and cancellation condition.
The revised and redirected payments form part of the Supreme Court's explanation for the new intended underlessor-underlessee relationship.
The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's merely altered rent explanation, although not its ultimate disposition.
The respondents' proposed assignment of Kumar's reversion was incompatible with the Supreme Court's finding that Kumar retained the reversion.
The contemplated perpetual underlease would ordinarily engage section 17(1)(d), but the express condition prevented the agreement from creating an immediate interest at execution.
The Judicial Committee's actual-demise and present-interest test supplies the legal standard adopted by the Supreme Court. It does not establish historical payment or possession.
The 1923 date places the compromise within the pre-1930 version of the judicial-decree exception, including its treatment of property outside the original suit.
The Supreme Court's conclusion about section 17 supplies the reason for dismissing the registration appeal. The dismissal itself is not evidence that the contractual payment condition was fulfilled.
Proof of an express condition is not proof of the later event required to satisfy it. The actual payment remains unknown on the supplied reasoning.
The purchaser's later recovery action establishes the assertion of derivative monetary rights, not independently every factual prerequisite for those rights.
The appellate issue was registration and admissibility, restricting what the Supreme Court's final order can properly be used to prove.

all_limitations: This is an unverified model reconstruction grounded exclusively in the supplied judgment for case 136109. It is not a certified factual record or a human gold annotation.

The Supreme Court's judgment text states that Patanjali Sastri J. delivered the judgment. The frontmatter contains an inconsistent author attribution to Hiralal J. Kania; substantive reasoning has therefore been attributed according to the judgment body.
The principal dispute concerns coal rights in the 500-bigha portion of a larger 5,800-bigha lease, with the original title litigation, the 1923 compromise, and the later recovery suit kept distinct.
The text renders the year of the execution sale as '193S'. No exact corrected year is inferred.

One sentence in the court's description of the possession restriction renders the disputed area as '503 bighas'. The repeatedly specified subject of the original title suit and underlease is 500 bighas. The textual discrepancy has not been treated as a separate property transaction.

The headnote contains irregular clause lettering in the supplied rendering. The operative reasoning of the judgment expressly identifies section 17(1)(d), section 17(1)(b), and section 17(2)(vi); those are the provisions reconstructed.

Descriptions of the compromise's rights, tenancy terms, financial obligations, and substitute-instrument clause establish what the compromise provided. They do not automatically establish performance, vesting, execution, or possession.

The judicial observation that the Singhs had not already obtained possession concerns the situation at or before the 1923 compromise. It is not evidence that they never obtained any later possessory right.

The High Court's account of the Deoshis continuing in possession is preserved as reported lower-court reasoning, not converted into an independent Supreme Court determination about all subsequent possession.
The Full Bench principle reported through the High Court in Charu Chandra Mitra's case is distinguished from the Supreme Court's rejection of the High Court's application to this compromise.

The Judicial Committee's Hemanta Kumari Debi precedent is used solely for the legal propositions the Supreme Court attributes to it: actual demise and immediate interest for an agreement to lease, and the pre-amendment scope of the decree exception. No target-case event is inferred from the precedent.

The respondents' assignment-and-attornment account and the appellant's altered-royalty registration argument are preserved as attributed submissions, not automatically as established facts or correct legal conclusions.

The Supreme Court affirmatively rejected the alleged assignment of Kumar's reversion through this compromise. This is a substantive interpretation of the target instrument, not simply a failure of documentary proof.

The initial absence of a present and immediate interest is established by the conditional terms as construed by the court. Whether the prescribed payment was actually made within two months remains unknown rather than false.

The apparent grant of a declaration of the Singhs' title under the compromise cannot be separated from its express conditional provisions and treated as proof of an unconditional proprietary entitlement.
The 1930 statutory amendment is considered only to determine its nonapplication to the 1923 decree. No general result for all post-amendment compromises is proposed.
The fact that the compromise covers the additional 5,300 bighas is relevant to the exception from registration, not proof of a separate new underlease involving that entire additional area.

The later purchaser's suit proves the assertion of a claim under the compromise. Its success below and the dismissal of the registration appeal are not used circularly to establish the historic satisfaction of the payment condition or every installment of royalty.

The judgment records that the lower courts decreed the recovery suit, but the Supreme Court's material appellate reasoning does not separately verify the arithmetic of arrears, the details of cess calculations, or all defenses unrelated to registration.
Rule operators are OPEN_TEXT except for the narrowly sourced conjunction in R3. No unstated all-or-any inference, additional statutory exception, or general doctrinal rule is supplied.

Evidence-use judgments assess whether a particular record supports the specified proposition. They are separate from the proposed truth state of the complete premise, and an attributed assertion can be usable as an assertion while unusable as proof of its underlying occurrence.
The final appellate dismissal is recorded as a disposition and not used as a premise establishing property ownership, physical possession, payment, or unconditional tenancy entitlement.

all_original_uses.basis: Both pattas are expressly described in the undisputed background. Together they establish the overlapping grants that led to the title dispute.

bindings.revised_royalty: 2 annas 6 pies per ton payable to the Singhs

all_original_uses.basis: The decree text identifies the proposed tenancy and the Supreme Court identifies the corresponding change in the royalty obligation. The combined evidence covers the full premise.
opposition: F12 presents the High Court's narrower characterization as a continuation of existing tenancy with altered payment arrangements.
gaps: The decree terms remain subject to the payment condition.

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court expressly characterizes the intended relationship as a perpetual underlease. This is usable to reconstruct the court's interpretation, not as independent evidence that the conditional transaction became effective.
opposition: F12 contains the different High Court characterization.
F14 contains the respondents' assignment-and-attornment alternative.
gaps: Satisfaction of the condition remains unestablished.

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court directly finds that Kumar retained his reversion and the Singhs continued as his tenants. This defeats the proposed assignment characterization.
opposition: F14 records counsel's contrary assignment theory.

all_original_uses.basis: The compromise contains hereditary-tenancy language and the Supreme Court expressly identifies the intended arrangement as a perpetual underlease. The court states that this arrangement would fall under section 17(1)(d) but for the condition.
gaps: The premise concerns the intended duration, not immediate legal operation.

all_original_uses.basis: The express restriction on execution and possession, combined with the Supreme Court's finding that the underlease was uncertain until payment, affirmatively negates present and immediate operation at execution. This is not an inference from the mere absence of a payment record.
opposition: F7 contains language declaring rights and describing hereditary tenancy, but those terms cannot be isolated from the condition.
gaps: The judgment does not determine whether the underlease subsequently became effective after payment.

all_original_uses.basis: The compromise expressly couples timely payment with cancellation, execution restrictions, and possession restrictions. These are the operative conditions on which the Supreme Court relies.
gaps: Whether the Singhs actually paid remains unknown.

all_original_uses.basis: The High Court's statement that the Deoshis continued in possession addresses continuity of physical occupation and its own view of the tenancy. It does not establish that the compromise immediately effected a new demise, and the Supreme Court rejected the High Court's simplified legal analysis.
opposition: F6 and F18 directly establish the condition preventing an immediate legal interest.
gaps: Continued physical occupation and immediate creation of a new proprietary interest are distinct propositions.

all_original_uses.basis: The undisputed history records the compromise by all parties and entry of a judicial decree on the same day.

The Supreme Court expressly classifies the contingent instrument under clause (b), rather than clause (d). This is a recorded judicial application, not independent proof of subsequent contractual performance and not reliance on the final dismissal as a premise.
opposition: F13 reports the appellant's asserted clause (d) classification.

all_original_uses.basis: The dated decree and the Supreme Court's treatment of the amendment together establish why the later statutory restriction was not applicable.
gaps: The decision does not establish how a materially different decree created after the amendment would be resolved in all circumstances.

all_original_uses.basis: The first patta establishes the total area, the title suit establishes its disputed portion, and the Supreme Court expressly identifies the remaining 5,300 bighas as outside the original suit. Together they fully establish this subject-matter distinction.

bindings.legal_issue: Whether altered rent creates a new lease under section 17(1)(d)

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court quotes the High Court's reliance on the Full Bench principle. This establishes the legal reasoning the High Court invoked, without adopting its application as correct.
opposition: F15 records the Supreme Court's disagreement with the High Court's characterization.

bindings.parties: The Singhs, the Deoshis, and Kumar

all_original_uses.basis: The High Court's analysis supplies a real contrary interpretation, but cannot establish as an accepted target-case finding that the compromise changed only rent. The Supreme Court expressly rejected that application.
gaps: The reported Full Bench principle is not itself disproved merely because the Supreme Court found it inappropriate for this transaction.

bindings.parties: The Singhs, the Deoshis, and Kumar

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court finds that the transaction did considerably more than alter rates: it contemplated a new underlessor-underlessee relationship. This directly negates the proposition that only rent terms changed.
opposition: F12 records the High Court's different assessment.

all_original_uses.basis: The quoted High Court reasoning expressly attributes the registration argument based on altered commission to the appellant's advocate. It proves the argument was made, not that the proposed legal classification was correct.
opposition: F19 gives the Supreme Court's contrary classification.

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court explicitly attributes the assignment-and-attornment explanation to respondents' counsel. This is reliable for identifying the litigated alternative.
gaps: No actual assignment is established by the attributed submission.

all_original_uses.basis: Counsel's assertion is not evidence that Kumar actually assigned his reversion. Moreover, the Supreme Court affirmatively rejects that characterization.
gaps: This judgment does not address all imaginable later assignments independently of the 1923 compromise.

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court concludes that Kumar retained his reversion over the full area and therefore could not be treated as having assigned the alleged landlord interest to the Singhs through the compromise.

The original lease establishes the head tenancy, the revised terms preserve the Singhs' payment obligations to Kumar, and the Supreme Court expressly determines that Kumar's reversion remained intact. The evidence bundle supports both the underlying arrangement and its adopted legal interpretation.
opposition: F14 presents the rejected assignment account.

all_original_uses.basis: The express compromise terms establish the legal condition and the specified consequences of nonperformance.
gaps: The consequence of nonpayment cannot be treated as actually triggered without evidence of nonpayment.

all_original_uses.basis: The decree proves that payment was required; it does not establish that payment occurred. The Supreme Court's analysis addresses contingency at the time of execution, not a factual finding of subsequent payment or nonpayment.
gaps: No payment date is established.
No finding that the Singhs failed to pay within the specified period is established.
The condition cannot be marked satisfied or breached from this evidence.

all_original_uses.basis: F9 specifies what documents were to be executed or substituted, and F10 shows subsequent purchase of the Singhs' interest and a recovery claim. Neither proves the actual satisfaction of the payment condition, execution of new instruments, or a particular postcondition change of possession.
gaps: Actual execution of the proposed new patta is not established.
Actual execution of the proposed Kabuliyat is not established.
The substitute-instrument provision does not prove that its prerequisites arose.
The precise postcondition possessory position is not independently established.

bindings.contested_issue: Whether nonregistration rendered the decree inadmissible

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court expressly limits the material plea in the appeal to registration and evidentiary admissibility.
gaps: The judgment does not state that all conceivable underlying contractual questions were finally retried.

bindings.lower_courts: Subordinate Judge, District Judge and Patna High Court in the recorded procedural history
bindings.claim: Royalties and cesses for Pous 1345 to Asadh 1349 B.S.

all_original_uses.basis: F10 establishes the nature and period of the claim. F1 establishes that the courts below gave effect to the compromise and decreed the suit. This supports the procedural outcome without independently proving every constituent debt fact.
gaps: The judgment excerpt does not provide a separate computation of arrears.
The outcome of the lower-court litigation should not be used as independent proof that the condition precedent was fulfilled.

all_opposition.issue: Whether Ex. 181 proved a signed agreement with ascertainable lease terms.
all_opposition.description: The Bombay High Court rejected the evidence as insufficient; the Supreme Court assessed the same documentary material differently and expressly rejected the High Court's analysis. These are different judicial evaluations of the same transaction, not separate contractual events.

all_opposition.issue: Fifty-year lease, permanent tenancy and effect of nonregistration.
all_opposition.description: The plaintiffs' pleading characterized the arrangement as a fifty-year negotiation and argued that no registered deed meant trespass. The Supreme Court instead construed the arrangement as permanent with rental revision after fifty years and applied section 53-A despite nonregistration.

all_opposition.issue: Whether physical entry preceded Government sanction.
all_opposition.description: The Talukdari Settlement Officer's recital establishes his assertion that permission was granted. It does not independently establish actual possession before sanction. The Supreme Court assessed the contrary circumstances and treated premature possession as unproved while accepting subsequent possession in part performance.

all_opposition.issue: Whether the respondent firm could maintain ejectment.
all_opposition.description: The Assistant Judge found the plaintiffs' standing unproved, while the High Court relied on claimed derivative interests, rent recognition, and receiver capacity. The Supreme Court's selection of section 53-A as dispositive left those competing standing analyses unresolved.

all_opposition.issue: Ex. 181's evidentiary weight versus the irregular timing of admission.
all_opposition.description: The Supreme Court considered Ex. 181 reliable secondary evidence even though its introduction after remand was procedurally improper. The exhibit's survival in the appellate record and its substantive reliability are separate determinations. The lateness affected costs.

all_opposition.issue: Independent lease-related action versus part-performance defence.
all_opposition.description: The Court excluded section 27-A because of its stated date restriction but applied section 53-A to protect possession. The unavailable independent-action route did not extinguish the defensive entitlement.

The initial factory-lease narrative identifies survey Nos. 228, 225 and 226, whereas the suit and operative dispute identify Nos. 222, 223, 225 and 226. The supplied judgment does not expressly reconcile these enumerations. The model does not silently correct one to match the other.

all_opposition.issue: Relationship between reasons and final order.
all_opposition.description: The section 53-A factual and evidentiary determinations explain why the Assistant Judge's dismissal was restored. The fact that the Supreme Court ultimately allowed the appeal does not independently prove any underlying statutory premise.

The plaintiffs' acquisition of described interests and the defendant's objection to their sufficiency are supported by the narrative. Those facts must not be collapsed into either a final finding of complete title or a finding that plaintiffs possessed no rights.

all_limitations: Only the complete supplied judgment identified as IK-885778 and source_ref_id turn0file0 was used. No external cases, searches, prior reviews, or conversations were consulted.

The judgment was delivered by the Supreme Court of India on 21 March 1950. The restored Assistant Judge's decision, the Bombay High Court's contrary second-appeal judgment, and the original trial judgment retain distinct court levels and procedural statuses.
The statutory rule quoted in the judgment contains ellipses. R1 follows the stated conjunctions and the Court's actual application without claiming to reconstruct omitted legislative text.
The statutory part-performance requirements are distinguished from the evidentiary rule applied to Ex. 181. A fact supportive of one component is not automatically sufficient for a compound premise.
A negotiated agreement to lease, an executed registered lease, and a statutory defence founded upon part performance are not equivalent legal objects.
The absence of a registered formal lease is established, but it does not establish absence of a written contract or prove trespass.

The Supreme Court's finding that an agreement was completed is based on its assessment of the written offer, acceptance, Government sanction and supporting evidence, not inferred from the appellate result.

The original lessee's receipt of permission to enter before Government sanction and his actual physical entry are separate events or propositions. The former was recited by the official; the latter's premature occurrence was not proved.
The Court did not give an exact physical possession date, and its rejection of the early-possession argument should not be converted into a fabricated calendar date.
The plaintiff's description of a fifty-year lease is preserved as a pleading. The Supreme Court's adopted construction concerned permanent tenancy and revision of rent after fifty years.
The distinct survey-number lists in the factual narrative and ejectment suit are preserved without silent correction or extrapolation.
The 1924 mortgage and 1933 acquisition of the equity of redemption are separate transactions; they explain the appellant's succession without implying an independently executed registered lease.
The mortgage schedule included property beyond the factory. No unsupported conclusion about every scheduled asset is drawn from the mortgage description.
The respondents' status as ijaradars and assignees of mortgage rights is reported, but the adequacy of those interests to maintain ejectment is not conclusively determined by the Supreme Court.
Rent acceptance is supported as conduct and contractual performance; its complete effect on ownership, standing or landlord estoppel is not automatically determined.

The Assistant Judge's and Bombay High Court's opposing standing analyses remain historically distinct. The Supreme Court's decision on section 53-A does not retrospectively convert either analysis into a final Supreme Court holding.
The pleaded allegation of a 25 December 1930 notice is not treated as independent proof that legally sufficient notice was served.
The High Court's refusal to entertain the proper-notice issue is a procedural disposition, not a merits ruling that notice was unnecessary or valid.
The remand issues concerning mortgagee occupation and non-joinder are preserved as issues raised. Their presence does not establish any final Supreme Court merits holding on those questions.
Ex. 181's reliability as secondary evidence is distinct from the admitted procedural impropriety of producing it after remand.

The Supreme Court's statement about primary correspondence being in the plaintiffs' or talukdars' possession or power is preserved as its evidentiary assessment, not supplemented by invented locations, custody dates, or copies.
Section 27-A of the Specific Relief Act is retained only in the scope expressly discussed by the Court. Its temporal inapplicability does not displace the section 53-A defence.
The express-contractual-right exception to section 53-A is preserved. The failure to establish an applicable exception here is not treated as proof that no express rights or reservations could exist.
The judgment did not order execution or registration of a formal lease. Remaining formal obligations and any possible affirmative remedy are not resolved merely by the dismissal of ejectment.

The headnote summarizes the decision but is not used as an independent factual basis superseding the Supreme Court's detailed reasoning. Its broad reference to continued rent collection is not substituted for the specific pleaded admission through 31 July 1932.

Neither the dismissal of the ejectment suit nor the rejection of a particular legal claim establishes that all possible rival ownership, tenancy, mortgage, notice, or contractual rights are nonexistent.
The case-specific refusal to reverse the Assistant Judge in second appeal is preserved without constructing a general second-appeal doctrine beyond the judgment's express reasoning.
The costs disposition was influenced by late documentary production and procedural irregularity. It is not treated as proof or disproof of the underlying agreement.
The final-order fact is used only to describe procedural outcome, never as a premise proving the section 53-A requirements.

All premises, evidence-to-premise judgments, polarity assessments and conclusions are proposed reconstructions. USABLE, UNUSABLE and UNRESOLVED describe the identified evidentiary use; TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN and CONFLICTED describe the distinct premise-state proposal.

bindings.transferor: Talukdari Settlement Officer acting for the Government-managed estate with Government sanction
bindings.land: lease lands treated by the Court as the suit lands, subject to the survey-number discrepancy
bindings.writing: signed offer, signed acceptance and signed Government sanction as evidenced by Ex. 181

all_original_uses.basis: The signed offer supplies the proposal and consideration; the Settlement Officer's signed acceptance and Government's signed sanction supply the authorized agreement; Ex. 181 and the Supreme Court's evidentiary findings establish those writings notwithstanding nonproduction of their originals.
gaps: The judgment's initial survey-number recital differs from the four-field enumeration in the suit.

all_original_uses.basis: The High Court's assertion that the correspondence was not evidence of the statutory written contract is usable to reconstruct its contrary reasoning, but not to establish nonexistence of that contract after the Supreme Court's contrary evidentiary determination.
gaps: The High Court's negative evidentiary assessment does not itself prove that the writings never existed.

all_original_uses.basis: The absence of an executed registered deed does not disprove an antecedent signed agreement. The trial court's treatment of an unproduced written lease as nonexistent cannot be substituted for the Supreme Court's determination based on Ex. 181.
gaps: The proposed inference confuses the registered formal lease with the underlying contract to lease.

bindings.land: survey lands treated as the subject of the agreement
bindings.terms: permanent tenancy, Rs. 290 annual rent and possible rental revision after fifty years

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court expressly identified the character of the tenancy, annual rent, and fifty-year rental-review term as reasonably deducible from the reliable official evidence.
gaps: The judgment does not reproduce every contractual condition, so this is the Court's determination of sufficient ascertainability rather than a reconstruction of a complete deed.

all_original_uses.basis: The High Court considered the terms insufficiently ascertainable. This is a material adverse interpretation, but the Supreme Court specifically rejected it after assessing Ex. 181.
gaps: The High Court's conclusion cannot be treated as an independent finding that no ascertainable terms existed.

bindings.terms: plaintiffs' characterization of fifty years at Rs. 290 annually

all_original_uses.basis: The plaint's admission of negotiations and rent is corroborative but cannot alone establish the complete signed agreement or prove that the tenancy expired after fifty years. The Supreme Court instead read the fifty years as a rental-review interval.
gaps: No independent determination of termination after fifty years follows from the pleading.

bindings.possession_event: entry and occupation pursuant to the arrangement

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court accepted possession in performance of the agreement and rejected the suggestion that actual possession had been proved to precede sanction. Existing tenants and the required arrangements informed its timing assessment.
gaps: The precise day possession commenced was not established.

all_original_uses.basis: The official's statement about permission to enter and the later argument about actual early possession are not equivalent. The statement did not independently establish when possession occurred, and the Supreme Court found the asserted premature entry unproved.
gaps: Permission to enter is not itself evidence that physical possession was actually delivered on that date.
Failure to prove early possession does not prove the historical impossibility of any earlier entry.

bindings.act: erection of factory, bungalow, engine rooms and other structures

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court treated substantial factory and related construction following the agreement as conduct in furtherance of the contemplated industrial lease.

bindings.act: tender and payment of agreed rent accepted by successive managers and plaintiffs

all_original_uses.basis: The agreed rent was tendered and repeatedly received, including by the respondent plaintiffs. The pleading admission supplies additional confirmation of performance under the arrangement.
gaps: The plaintiffs' express pleading admission specifically covers payments through 31 July 1932; later acceptance is not inferred from that admission alone.

bindings.obligations: rent and other transferee-side contractual performance

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court expressly found willingness and actual performance on the lessee's side. The outstanding execution and registration of the deed were acts to be completed on the lessor side and did not negate this finding.
gaps: The finding does not establish that the formal lease was eventually executed.

all_original_uses.basis: The missing formal registered lease cannot by itself establish that the transferee was unwilling or failed to perform his side of the agreement.
gaps: Absence of the executed deed does not identify which party was unwilling or determine the performance status of other obligations.

bindings.claimant: respondent firm claiming through talukdari-side interests
bindings.respondent_to_claim: Sheth Maneklal Mansukhbhai as mortgagee and successor to the original lessee

all_original_uses.basis: The respondents asserted derivative interests on the lessor side and sought recovery from a defendant who succeeded to the original lessee's rights. The premise concerns the nature of the opposing claims, not a final determination that the respondents possessed valid title or standing.
gaps: Whether plaintiffs actually had complete title or standing was not decided by the Supreme Court.

all_original_uses.basis: The defendant challenged plaintiffs' derivative title and the Assistant Judge agreed they had not established standing. gaps: A final Supreme Court determination of plaintiffs' complete title, mortgage-assignee rights, or standing is absent.

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court found the original papers to have been in the possession or power of the plaintiffs or their predecessors and withheld despite notice; the plaintiffs' knowledge was inferred from their pleadings and testimony.

bindings.procedural_defect: late production and improper post-remand admission

all_original_uses.basis: The exhibit was admitted following remand despite the limited remand issues. The Supreme Court expressly described this admission as improper, but recognized that the High Court had not rejected the document and that it could not be excluded at the final appellate stage.
gaps: The procedural survival of the exhibit must not be represented as a holding that its admission after remand was initially proper.

all_original_uses.basis: The arrangement was made and sanctioned in 1917, before the cutoff specified for section 27-A of the Specific Relief Act. The Court expressly held that provision inapplicable, while preserving the separate section 53-A defence.
gaps: No conclusion on other hypothetical section 27-A requirements is necessary.

all_original_uses.basis: The High Court regarded rent recognition and alternative capacities as sufficient for suit standing. gaps: The Supreme Court did not decide whether any single asserted capacity was sufficient.

bindings.claimed_capacities: ijaradar, mortgage assignee and recognized landlord

all_original_uses.basis: The Assistant Judge found plaintiffs' legal standing unproved, while the Bombay High Court reached a contrary view on multiple theories. gaps: The source supplies no final Supreme Court merits resolution of the opposing standing theories.

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court expressly reported that the proper-notice argument had not been raised in either lower court, explaining the High Court's refusal to allow it at second appeal.

gaps: No individual private settlement date or tenant-ejectment notice date is established.

all_original_uses.basis: The plaintiffs' own pleading acknowledged negotiations through correspondence and the proposed rental consideration. That admission corroborated the transaction but did not alone establish the required signed acceptance, official sanction, and complete statutory written-contract premise. Those elements were established through the separate Ex. 181 evidence chain.
gaps: The pleading alone does not identify and prove every required signature.
Its characterization of a fifty-year lease differs from the Supreme Court's interpretation of a permanent lease with rent revisable after fifty years.

The judgment was delivered by the Supreme Court of India on 21 March 1950. The restored Assistant Judge's decision, the Bombay High Court's contrary second-appeal judgment, and the original trial judgment retain distinct court levels and procedural statuses.
The statutory rule quoted in the judgment contains ellipses. R1 follows the stated conjunctions and the Court's actual application without claiming to reconstruct omitted legislative text.
The statutory part-performance requirements are distinguished from the evidentiary rule applied to Ex. 181. A fact supportive of one component is not automatically sufficient for a compound premise.
A negotiated agreement to lease, an executed registered lease, and a statutory defence founded upon part performance are not equivalent legal objects.
The absence of a registered formal lease is established, but it does not establish absence of a written contract or prove trespass.

The Supreme Court's finding that an agreement was completed is based on its assessment of the written offer, acceptance, Government sanction and supporting evidence, not inferred from the appellate result.

The original lessee's receipt of permission to enter before Government sanction and his actual physical entry are separate events or propositions. The former was recited by the official; the latter's premature occurrence was not proved.
The Court did not give an exact physical possession date, and its rejection of the early-possession argument should not be converted into a fabricated calendar date.
The plaintiff's description of a fifty-year lease is preserved as a pleading. The Supreme Court's adopted construction concerned permanent tenancy and revision of rent after fifty years.
The distinct survey-number lists in the factual narrative and ejectment suit are preserved without silent correction or extrapolation.
The 1924 mortgage and 1933 acquisition of the equity of redemption are separate transactions; they explain the appellant's succession without implying an independently executed registered lease.
The mortgage schedule included property beyond the factory. No unsupported conclusion about every scheduled asset is drawn from the mortgage description.
The respondents' status as ijaradars and assignees of mortgage rights is reported, but the adequacy of those interests to maintain ejectment is not conclusively determined by the Supreme Court.
Rent acceptance is supported as conduct and contractual performance; its complete effect on ownership, standing or landlord estoppel is not automatically determined.

The Assistant Judge's and Bombay High Court's opposing standing analyses remain historically distinct. The Supreme Court's decision on section 53-A does not retrospectively convert either analysis into a final Supreme Court holding.
The pleaded allegation of a 25 December 1930 notice is not treated as independent proof that legally sufficient notice was served.
The High Court's refusal to entertain the proper-notice issue is a procedural disposition, not a merits ruling that notice was unnecessary or valid.
The remand issues concerning mortgagee occupation and non-joinder are preserved as issues raised. Their presence does not establish any final Supreme Court merits holding on those questions.
Ex. 181's reliability as secondary evidence is distinct from the admitted procedural impropriety of producing it after remand.

The Supreme Court's statement about primary correspondence being in the plaintiffs' or talukdars' possession or power is preserved as its evidentiary assessment, not supplemented by invented locations, custody dates, or copies.
Section 27-A of the Specific Relief Act is retained only in the scope expressly discussed by the Court. Its temporal inapplicability does not displace the section 53-A defence.
The express-contractual-right exception to section 53-A is preserved. The failure to establish an applicable exception here is not treated as proof that no express rights or reservations could exist.
The judgment did not order execution or registration of a formal lease. Remaining formal obligations and any possible affirmative remedy are not resolved merely by the dismissal of ejectment.

The headnote summarizes the decision but is not used as an independent factual basis superseding the Supreme Court's detailed reasoning. Its broad reference to continued rent collection is not substituted for the specific pleaded admission through 31 July 1932.

Neither the dismissal of the ejectment suit nor the rejection of a particular legal claim establishes that all possible rival ownership, tenancy, mortgage, notice, or contractual rights are nonexistent.
The case-specific refusal to reverse the Assistant Judge in second appeal is preserved without constructing a general second-appeal doctrine beyond the judgment's express reasoning.
The costs disposition was influenced by late documentary production and procedural irregularity. It is not treated as proof or disproof of the underlying agreement.
The final-order fact is used only to describe procedural outcome, never as a premise proving the section 53-A requirements.

The judgment was delivered by the Supreme Court of India on 21 March 1950. The restored Assistant Judge's decision, the Bombay High Court's contrary second-appeal judgment, and the original trial judgment retain distinct court levels and procedural statuses.
The statutory rule quoted in the judgment contains ellipses. R1 follows the stated conjunctions and the Court's actual application without claiming to reconstruct omitted legislative text.
The statutory part-performance requirements are distinguished from the evidentiary rule applied to Ex. 181. A fact supportive of one component is not automatically sufficient for a compound premise.
A negotiated agreement to lease, an executed registered lease, and a statutory defence founded upon part performance are not equivalent legal objects.
The absence of a registered formal lease is established, but it does not establish absence of a written contract or prove trespass.

The Supreme Court's finding that an agreement was completed is based on its assessment of the written offer, acceptance, Government sanction and supporting evidence, not inferred from the appellate result.

The original lessee's receipt of permission to enter before Government sanction and his actual physical entry are separate events or propositions. The former was recited by the official; the latter's premature occurrence was not proved.
The Court did not give an exact physical possession date, and its rejection of the early-possession argument should not be converted into a fabricated calendar date.
The plaintiff's description of a fifty-year lease is preserved as a pleading. The Supreme Court's adopted construction concerned permanent tenancy and revision of rent after fifty years.
The distinct survey-number lists in the factual narrative and ejectment suit are preserved without silent correction or extrapolation.
The 1924 mortgage and 1933 acquisition of the equity of redemption are separate transactions; they explain the appellant's succession without implying an independently executed registered lease.
The mortgage schedule included property beyond the factory. No unsupported conclusion about every scheduled asset is drawn from the mortgage description.
The respondents' status as ijaradars and assignees of mortgage rights is reported, but the adequacy of those interests to maintain ejectment is not conclusively determined by the Supreme Court.
Rent acceptance is supported as conduct and contractual performance; its complete effect on ownership, standing or landlord estoppel is not automatically determined.

The Assistant Judge's and Bombay High Court's opposing standing analyses remain historically distinct. The Supreme Court's decision on section 53-A does not retrospectively convert either analysis into a final Supreme Court holding.
The pleaded allegation of a 25 December 1930 notice is not treated as independent proof that legally sufficient notice was served.
The High Court's refusal to entertain the proper-notice issue is a procedural disposition, not a merits ruling that notice was unnecessary or valid.
The remand issues concerning mortgagee occupation and non-joinder are preserved as issues raised. Their presence does not establish any final Supreme Court merits holding on those questions.
Ex. 181's reliability as secondary evidence is distinct from the admitted procedural impropriety of producing it after remand.

The Supreme Court's statement about primary correspondence being in the plaintiffs' or talukdars' possession or power is preserved as its evidentiary assessment, not supplemented by invented locations, custody dates, or copies.
Section 27-A of the Specific Relief Act is retained only in the scope expressly discussed by the Court. Its temporal inapplicability does not displace the section 53-A defence.
The express-contractual-right exception to section 53-A is preserved. The failure to establish an applicable exception here is not treated as proof that no express rights or reservations could exist.
The judgment did not order execution or registration of a formal lease. Remaining formal obligations and any possible affirmative remedy are not resolved merely by the dismissal of ejectment.

The headnote summarizes the decision but is not used as an independent factual basis superseding the Supreme Court's detailed reasoning. Its broad reference to continued rent collection is not substituted for the specific pleaded admission through 31 July 1932.

Neither the dismissal of the ejectment suit nor the rejection of a particular legal claim establishes that all possible rival ownership, tenancy, mortgage, notice, or contractual rights are nonexistent.
The case-specific refusal to reverse the Assistant Judge in second appeal is preserved without constructing a general second-appeal doctrine beyond the judgment's express reasoning.
The costs disposition was influenced by late documentary production and procedural irregularity. It is not treated as proof or disproof of the underlying agreement.
The final-order fact is used only to describe procedural outcome, never as a premise proving the section 53-A requirements.

The three premises concern distinct aspects of the same Ex. 181 evidentiary chain: official documentary reliability, custody and nonproduction of originals, and survival of an improperly admitted exhibit.
The underlying 1917 lease arrangement is treated as a written agreement to lease, not an executed registered lease deed.
The Supreme Court's evidentiary assessment of Ex. 181 is supported by the supplied judgment but does not constitute independent examination of the original signed correspondence.
The Bombay High Court's contrary assessment of the Government correspondence remains an attributed lower-court view. The Supreme Court expressly rejected that evidentiary conclusion.
The plaintiff's inability to identify the exact location of the correspondence is retained. It does not establish that the plaintiffs and talukdars lacked possession or power over the originals.

The Court's inference regarding the plaintiff's knowledge was described as prima facie. The precise physical custody and complete chain of custody of each original document were not independently established.
The after-remand production and admission of Ex. 181 were procedurally improper. Its continued availability at the Supreme Court stage does not validate its initial admission.
The 1938 remand concerned mortgagee occupation and non-joinder. These questions are retained as procedural context, not converted into determinations of the underlying merits.

The judgment was delivered by the Supreme Court of India on 21 March 1950. The restored Assistant Judge's decision, the Bombay High Court's contrary second-appeal judgment, and the original trial judgment retain distinct court levels and procedural statuses.
The statutory rule quoted in the judgment contains ellipses. R1 follows the stated conjunctions and the Court's actual application without claiming to reconstruct omitted legislative text.
The statutory part-performance requirements are distinguished from the evidentiary rule applied to Ex. 181. A fact supportive of one component is not automatically sufficient for a compound premise.
A negotiated agreement to lease, an executed registered lease, and a statutory defence founded upon part performance are not equivalent legal objects.
The absence of a registered formal lease is established, but it does not establish absence of a written contract or prove trespass.

The Supreme Court's finding that an agreement was completed is based on its assessment of the written offer, acceptance, Government sanction and supporting evidence, not inferred from the appellate result.

The original lessee's receipt of permission to enter before Government sanction and his actual physical entry are separate events or propositions. The former was recited by the official; the latter's premature occurrence was not proved.
The Court did not give an exact physical possession date, and its rejection of the early-possession argument should not be converted into a fabricated calendar date.
The plaintiff's description of a fifty-year lease is preserved as a pleading. The Supreme Court's adopted construction concerned permanent tenancy and revision of rent after fifty years.
The distinct survey-number lists in the factual narrative and ejectment suit are preserved without silent correction or extrapolation.
The 1924 mortgage and 1933 acquisition of the equity of redemption are separate transactions; they explain the appellant's succession without implying an independently executed registered lease.
The mortgage schedule included property beyond the factory. No unsupported conclusion about every scheduled asset is drawn from the mortgage description.
The respondents' status as ijaradars and assignees of mortgage rights is reported, but the adequacy of those interests to maintain ejectment is not conclusively determined by the Supreme Court.
Rent acceptance is supported as conduct and contractual performance; its complete effect on ownership, standing or landlord estoppel is not automatically determined.

The Assistant Judge's and Bombay High Court's opposing standing analyses remain historically distinct. The Supreme Court's decision on section 53-A does not retrospectively convert either analysis into a final Supreme Court holding.
The pleaded allegation of a 25 December 1930 notice is not treated as independent proof that legally sufficient notice was served.
The High Court's refusal to entertain the proper-notice issue is a procedural disposition, not a merits ruling that notice was unnecessary or valid.
The remand issues concerning mortgagee occupation and non-joinder are preserved as issues raised. Their presence does not establish any final Supreme Court merits holding on those questions.
Ex. 181's reliability as secondary evidence is distinct from the admitted procedural impropriety of producing it after remand.

The Supreme Court's statement about primary correspondence being in the plaintiffs' or talukdars' possession or power is preserved as its evidentiary assessment, not supplemented by invented locations, custody dates, or copies.
Section 27-A of the Specific Relief Act is retained only in the scope expressly discussed by the Court. Its temporal inapplicability does not displace the section 53-A defence.
The express-contractual-right exception to section 53-A is preserved. The failure to establish an applicable exception here is not treated as proof that no express rights or reservations could exist.
The judgment did not order execution or registration of a formal lease. Remaining formal obligations and any possible affirmative remedy are not resolved merely by the dismissal of ejectment.

The headnote summarizes the decision but is not used as an independent factual basis superseding the Supreme Court's detailed reasoning. Its broad reference to continued rent collection is not substituted for the specific pleaded admission through 31 July 1932.

Neither the dismissal of the ejectment suit nor the rejection of a particular legal claim establishes that all possible rival ownership, tenancy, mortgage, notice, or contractual rights are nonexistent.
The case-specific refusal to reverse the Assistant Judge in second appeal is preserved without constructing a general second-appeal doctrine beyond the judgment's express reasoning.
The costs disposition was influenced by late documentary production and procedural irregularity. It is not treated as proof or disproof of the underlying agreement.
The final-order fact is used only to describe procedural outcome, never as a premise proving the section 53-A requirements.

all_limitations: This is an unverified model reconstruction based exclusively on the supplied judgment in turn0file0. No external sources or other conversations were used.

The Court's rejection of a hypothetical composite construction does not deny the legal possibility of genuine surrender followed by a valid transfer from an heir.

all_original_limits: This is an unverified model reconstruction based exclusively on the supplied judgment in turn0file0. No external sources or other conversations were used.
The judgment is a Supreme Court appellate decision dated 8 May 1951; the trial and Madras High Court findings retain their respective stages and are not automatically Supreme Court findings.
The primary dispute concerns succession, surrender and recovery of property, not an independently adjudicated landlord-tenant entitlement.
All six schedule A items existed, but the Supreme Court appeal specifically concerned items 1, 4 and 5.
Exhibit P-6's terms and the parties' competing constructions are separately attributed; pleading a legal effect is not proof that the effect occurred.
A widow's putative release and later derivative sales are distinct events. The 1922 and 1929 sale deeds were not executed by Chanchamma herself.
The trial court's failure to find sufficient evidence excluding nearer heirs cannot be translated into an affirmative finding of an existing nearer heir.
The High Court's nearest-reversioner finding, rather than the mere plaintiffs' assertion or Supreme Court final order, provides the operative factual footing in the narrowed appeal.
Narasamma's death in 1926 and Chanchamma's death in March 1933 are separate legally significant events; their alternative limitation roles must not be conflated.
The absence of an effective surrender does not imply that Chanchamma never intended to relinquish management or confer a benefit.
The Court's rejection of a hypothetical composite construction does not deny the legal possibility of genuine surrender followed by a valid transfer from an heir.
The reported Nobokishore rule was assumed for present purposes rather than unreservedly approved; the Court expressly criticized its extension.
Reported precedent transactions are used solely to describe and evaluate legal reasoning, not to prove target-case events.
The possible rule of estoppel is expressly qualified and cannot be converted into either proven estoppel or proof that estoppel could never arise.
The separate izara lease and its stated Fasli expiry are document context only. No independent finding about actual lease termination or tenant entitlement is supplied.
The recognized Rs. 5,061 and odd annas represents the accepted estate-benefiting amount for item 1, not full validation of the Rs. 33,000 consideration.
No item 1 deposit completion, possession delivery, exact interest commencement dates, or quantified mesne profits may be inferred.
Article 141 and Article 125 are cited as discussed in this historical judgment; this reconstruction does not independently update or generalize statutory law.
The final appellate dismissal is recorded as disposition and is not used circularly as evidence proving entitlement.

TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN and CONFLICTED are premise-state proposals for the specified interpretive use; USABLE, UNUSABLE and UNRESOLVED separately concern whether particular evidence can establish that premise.

all_opposition.description: The plaintiff's asserted sale consideration and part-performance possession conflict with the defendants second party's loan and interest-facilitation explanation. They concern the same Rs. 30,000 and possession arrangement, not two separate transactions.
all_opposition.resolution: The trial and High Court accepted the loan explanation and rejected proof of the sale-based explanation.

all_opposition.description: The plaintiff attributed notice of the alleged prior sale contract to the later purchasers. The defendants first party denied notice, and both lower courts found that they purchased for value without notice.
all_opposition.resolution: The subsequent purchasers' value-without-notice account was accepted in the factual findings.

all_opposition.description: The High Court treated the absence of a loan prayer as barring the money decree. The Supreme Court distinguished that omission from the defendants' own express admission and absence of prejudice.
all_opposition.resolution: The pleading omission remained a fact, but its supposed absolute consequence was rejected.

all_opposition.description: The Judicial Committee's unpleaded restitution relief in a void-mortgage dispute was cited by analogy to justify non-prejudicial alternative relief. Its mortgage facts, section 65 foundation, and ex parte setting remain confined to that precedent.
all_opposition.resolution: Analogical support for the procedural principle only.

all_opposition.description: The cited Judicial Committee practice admits exceptional departure from concurrent factual findings. Its reported proposition does not establish any exceptional circumstance in the present case.
all_opposition.resolution: The Supreme Court found none in this appeal.

all_opposition.description: The alleged hundi tender and refusal were contested by the plaintiff's denial of receipt. The Supreme Court additionally doubted legal sufficiency even if the alleged events were assumed true.
all_opposition.resolution: The tender defence did not defeat later interest, but the Court did not make a final factual determination of delivery or a conclusive independent tender-validity finding.

all_opposition.description: The defendants pleaded 6% annual loan interest and the trial court initially granted 6% from the suit date. The Supreme Court instead excluded the period of possession and fixed 4% from 1 September 1943.
all_opposition.resolution: The operative post-possession interest measure is the Supreme Court's 4% determination, not the pleaded or original trial-court rate.

all_opposition.description: The source describes the alleged sale arrangement as occurring in late October 1945 but gives 28 October 1941 for payment under it, despite the reported later sale and 1943 lawsuit.
all_opposition.resolution: No correction inferred. The apparent inconsistency is preserved as a limitation of the rendered plaintiff-account chronology.

all_opposition.description: The final refusal of specific performance and limited money award result from factual findings, appellate restraint, procedural fairness, and interest assessment. The operative decree is not used as independent proof of the underlying loan, contract failure, or possession history.
all_opposition.resolution: Reasoning-to-disposition direction preserved.

all_limitations: Only the supplied judgment is used. No external authority, fact checking, prior answer, or other conversation contributes to this reconstruction.
All facts, rules, uses, interpretations and references are unverified model proposals rather than human-validated gold labels.
The frontmatter and headnote are not substituted for the Supreme Court's operative reasoning. The judgment's own reasoning controls where a narrower conclusion is required.

Party pleadings and counsel submissions are preserved as attributed statements. Their mere inclusion does not establish the underlying transaction, notice, payment route, delivery of an instrument, or legal entitlement.
The parties' competing sale-price and loan accounts concern one contested Rs. 30,000 transaction and associated possession arrangement. No second financial or possession event is invented.

The supplied narrative contains an apparent chronology inconsistency between the alleged late October 1945 contract and 28 October 1941 payment. It has not been silently corrected or used to manufacture a separate dispositive ground.

The plaintiff's allegation that payment was made to a creditor of the vendors is preserved as an allegation. The lower courts' accepted loan characterisation does not independently establish every detail of the asserted payment route.

A proposition that a concluded sale contract was established is marked FALSE because the courts expressly found it unproved. This does not establish that no negotiations, discussions, or related events occurred.
The defendants' explanation of possession is corroborated by judicial findings. Possession itself is not denied; its claimed character as sale-based part performance was rejected.

The finding that the defendants first party were purchasers for value without notice is a lower-court factual finding accepted within the appellate framework, not an inference based solely on their denial of notice.
The Supreme Court's ordinary restraint concerning concurrent factual findings admits the express exceptional categories discussed in the judgment. None was found applicable here.
The general pleading rule and the admitted-alternative relief principle are retained together. Neither an absolute no-unpleaded-relief prohibition nor an unlimited exception is inferred.

The Judicial Committee mortgage-restitution precedent remains a reported analogy. Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act is not invented as the operative source of the plaintiff's loan-repayment decree.
The Judicial Committee reference on concurrent findings remains precedent material, not proof of exceptional circumstances in the present case.
The High Court's vagueness and minor-prejudice reasoning is preserved as a conditional alternative, not attributed to the Supreme Court as an independently decisive holding.
The receipt of the alleged July 1943 hundi remains disputed. The plaintiff's denial does not prove non-delivery, and the defendants' assertion does not prove delivery or valid tender.
The Supreme Court's doubt about legal tender does not supply a complete rule defining valid tender. No additional statutory or doctrinal requirements are imported.
The interest start date is grounded in the admitted end-of-August 1943 possession boundary and the Court's own selection of 1 September 1943.
The original pleaded 6% rate, trial decree at 6%, High Court's uncertainty concerning interest payment, and Supreme Court's final 4% rate retain separate procedural and evidentiary statuses.
The final decree is not used as a circular factual premise. It is reported only as the consequence of the reconstructed reasoning.
The judgment does not separately adjudicate tenancy, independent continuing occupation, eviction, rent, comprehensive accounting, or an independent title declaration.
Unknown event dates, additional party identities, exact original pleading language, and independent evidence not contained in the supplied rendering are not supplied through guesswork.
The source supports qualitative OPEN_TEXT legal evaluations rather than exhaustive Boolean conjunctions or disjunctions. No unsupported ALL, ANY, or exception structure has been imposed.

Unproved is not equated with false as an underlying historical proposition; FALSE premise states are restricted to propositions expressly defeated or not established in the adjudicated legal and evidentiary context.
Unknown bindings are not filled by wildcard identities, invented actors, or assumed missing evidence.

The Supreme Court expressly identified loan recovery as an available alternative pleading and treated inconsistency with the sale-based claim as immaterial to its permissibility.

The Supreme Court expressly acknowledged that the plaintiff did not make the loan allegation in the plaint. This directly negates actual pleading, without negating the legal possibility of alternative pleading.

The High Court identified the omission as the basis for setting aside the money decree, and the Supreme Court agreed that the loan claim had not been pleaded while rejecting the High Court's ultimate procedural conclusion.

The defendants second party expressly advanced the loan account themselves. The Supreme Court concluded that a claim on that admission could cause no surprise or injustice. Accordingly, the proposition that they lacked a fair opportunity to meet the loan basis is false in the Court's application.

These records establish both components of the defendants' pleaded alternative: their express admission of the loan and their explanation that possession facilitated its interest payment. Their own account directly answered the plaintiff's sale theory.

The trial court made an affirmative finding that the money was advanced as a loan, and the High Court concurred. This is stronger than treating the defendants' pleading as automatically proving the underlying transaction.

F08 supplies the failure of the sale-contract case, while F16 supplies the plaintiff's failure to plead loan recovery. Together they cover the compound premise without treating either component as supplied by mere inference.

The Supreme Court made the no-surprise and no-injustice assessment expressly. The reported Judicial Committee analogy supports the Court's legal reasoning but is not necessary to prove what the target-case defendants pleaded.
The Supreme Court expressly recorded the cessation date as admitted, providing the temporal boundary of the earlier possession period.
gaps: The initial date of possession is not specified.

all_original_uses.basis: The Supreme Court recorded that the no-interest-during-possession objection was correct and not disputed by the plaintiff. The use is confined to that earlier period.
The record establishes that counsel asserted sending and refusal of the hundi. It does not prove either occurrence.

The Supreme Court explicitly recorded that the plaintiff denied receipt in both the plaint and the evidence. The denial is established as a litigation position, not as independent proof of non-receipt.

Counsel asserted tender and refusal, while the plaintiff denied receipt. These opposing statements do not establish actual delivery, receipt, refusal, or legal sufficiency. The Court's legal doubt does not amount to a definitive historical finding that no hundi was sent.
gaps: Actual transmission and delivery are not established by the supplied reasoning.
Actual refusal is not established.
The Court did not conclusively determine the legal validity of the alleged tender.

all_original_uses.basis: The Court explicitly questioned whether the alleged arrangement would constitute a valid tender even if the defendants' account were factually true. The use establishes the judicial evaluation and its conditional nature.
gaps: The Court did not supply an exhaustive legal test for valid tender.

all_original_uses.basis: The trial finding establishes the loan character of the Rs. 30,000 advance; the Supreme Court's reasoning supplies its assessment of the defendants' use of the money and the justification for some interest.

The admitted cessation of possession at the end of August 1943 supports treating 1 September 1943 as the beginning of the post-possession period. The exact rate is separately supplied by the Court's evaluation, not inferred from this fact.

The Supreme Court expressly recorded that counsel for both sides left the question of interest to its determination. The Court's subsequent choice of 4% is a legal and discretionary application, not a premise proved from the final order.

all_original_limits: Only the supplied judgment is used. No external authority, fact checking, prior answer, or other conversation contributes to this reconstruction.
All facts, rules, uses, interpretations and references are unverified model proposals rather than human-validated gold labels.
The frontmatter and headnote are not substituted for the Supreme Court's operative reasoning. The judgment's own reasoning controls where a narrower conclusion is required.

Party pleadings and counsel submissions are preserved as attributed statements. Their mere inclusion does not establish the underlying transaction, notice, payment route, delivery of an instrument, or legal entitlement.
The parties' competing sale-price and loan accounts concern one contested Rs. 30,000 transaction and associated possession arrangement. No second financial or possession event is invented.

The supplied narrative contains an apparent chronology inconsistency between the alleged late October 1945 contract and 28 October 1941 payment. It has not been silently corrected or used to manufacture a separate dispositive ground.

The plaintiff's allegation that payment was made to a creditor of the vendors is preserved as an allegation. The lower courts' accepted loan characterisation does not independently establish every detail of the asserted payment route.

A proposition that a concluded sale contract was established is marked FALSE because the courts expressly found it unproved. This does not establish that no negotiations, discussions, or related events occurred.
The defendants' explanation of possession is corroborated by judicial findings. Possession itself is not denied; its claimed character as sale-based part performance was rejected.

The finding that the defendants first party were purchasers for value without notice is a lower-court factual finding accepted within the appellate framework, not an inference based solely on their denial of notice.
The Supreme Court's ordinary restraint concerning concurrent factual findings admits the express exceptional categories discussed in the judgment. None was found applicable here.
The general pleading rule and the admitted-alternative relief principle are retained together. Neither an absolute no-unpleaded-relief prohibition nor an unlimited exception is inferred.

The Judicial Committee mortgage-restitution precedent remains a reported analogy. Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act is not invented as the operative source of the plaintiff's loan-repayment decree.
The Judicial Committee reference on concurrent findings remains precedent material, not proof of exceptional circumstances in the present case.
The High Court's vagueness and minor-prejudice reasoning is preserved as a conditional alternative, not attributed to the Supreme Court as an independently decisive holding.
The receipt of the alleged July 1943 hundi remains disputed. The plaintiff's denial does not prove non-delivery, and the defendants' assertion does not prove delivery or valid tender.
The Supreme Court's doubt about legal tender does not supply a complete rule defining valid tender. No additional statutory or doctrinal requirements are imported.
The interest start date is grounded in the admitted end-of-August 1943 possession boundary and the Court's own selection of 1 September 1943.
The original pleaded 6% rate, trial decree at 6%, High Court's uncertainty concerning interest payment, and Supreme Court's final 4% rate retain separate procedural and evidentiary statuses.
The final decree is not used as a circular factual premise. It is reported only as the consequence of the reconstructed reasoning.
The judgment does not separately adjudicate tenancy, independent continuing occupation, eviction, rent, comprehensive accounting, or an independent title declaration.
Unknown event dates, additional party identities, exact original pleading language, and independent evidence not contained in the supplied rendering are not supplied through guesswork.
The source supports qualitative OPEN_TEXT legal evaluations rather than exhaustive Boolean conjunctions or disjunctions. No unsupported ALL, ANY, or exception structure has been imposed.

Unproved is not equated with false as an underlying historical proposition; FALSE premise states are restricted to propositions expressly defeated or not established in the adjudicated legal and evidentiary context.
Unknown bindings are not filled by wildcard identities, invented actors, or assumed missing evidence.

all_opposition.description: The plaintiff's asserted sale consideration and part-performance possession conflict with the defendants second party's loan and interest-facilitation explanation. They concern the same Rs. 30,000 and possession arrangement, not two separate transactions.
all_opposition.resolution: The trial and High Court accepted the loan explanation and rejected proof of the sale-based explanation.

all_opposition.description: The plaintiff attributed notice of the alleged prior sale contract to the later purchasers. The defendants first party denied notice, and both lower courts found that they purchased for value without notice.
all_opposition.resolution: The subsequent purchasers' value-without-notice account was accepted in the factual findings.

all_opposition.description: The High Court treated the absence of a loan prayer as barring the money decree. The Supreme Court distinguished that omission from the defendants' own express admission and absence of prejudice.
all_opposition.resolution: The pleading omission remained a fact, but its supposed absolute consequence was rejected.

all_opposition.description: The Judicial Committee's unpleaded restitution relief in a void-mortgage dispute was cited by analogy to justify non-prejudicial alternative relief. Its mortgage facts, section 65 foundation, and ex parte setting remain confined to that precedent.
all_opposition.resolution: Analogical support for the procedural principle only.

all_opposition.description: The cited Judicial Committee practice admits exceptional departure from concurrent factual findings. Its reported proposition does not establish any exceptional circumstance in the present case.
all_opposition.resolution: The Supreme Court found none in this appeal.

all_opposition.description: The alleged hundi tender and refusal were contested by the plaintiff's denial of receipt. The Supreme Court additionally doubted legal sufficiency even if the alleged events were assumed true.
all_opposition.resolution: The tender defence did not defeat later interest, but the Court did not make a final factual determination of delivery or a conclusive independent tender-validity finding.

all_opposition.description: The defendants pleaded 6% annual loan interest and the trial court initially granted 6% from the suit date. The Supreme Court instead excluded the period of possession and fixed 4% from 1 September 1943.
all_opposition.resolution: The operative post-possession interest measure is the Supreme Court's 4% determination, not the pleaded or original trial-court rate.

all_opposition.description: The source describes the alleged sale arrangement as occurring in late October 1945 but gives 28 October 1941 for payment under it, despite the reported later sale and 1943 lawsuit.
all_opposition.resolution: No correction inferred. The apparent inconsistency is preserved as a limitation of the rendered plaintiff-account chronology.

all_original_opposition.resolution: The trial and High Court accepted the loan explanation and rejected proof of the sale-based explanation.

all_original_opposition.description: The plaintiff attributed notice of the alleged prior sale contract to the later purchasers. The defendants first party denied notice, and both lower courts found that they purchased for value without notice.
all_original_opposition.resolution: The subsequent purchasers' value-without-notice account was accepted in the factual findings.

all_original_opposition.description: The High Court treated the absence of a loan prayer as barring the money decree. The Supreme Court distinguished that omission from the defendants' own express admission and absence of prejudice.
all_original_opposition.resolution: The pleading omission remained a fact, but its supposed absolute consequence was rejected.

all_original_opposition.description: The cited Judicial Committee practice admits exceptional departure from concurrent factual findings. Its reported proposition does not establish any exceptional circumstance in the present case.
all_original_opposition.resolution: The Supreme Court found none in this appeal.

all_original_opposition.description: The alleged hundi tender and refusal were contested by the plaintiff's denial of receipt. The Supreme Court additionally doubted legal sufficiency even if the alleged events were assumed true.
all_original_opposition.resolution: The tender defence did not defeat later interest, but the Court did not make a final factual determination of delivery or a conclusive independent tender-validity finding.

gaps: No established sale agreement to which part performance could be attributed.

all_original_uses.basis: The defendants' loan-interest explanation was contrary to the plaintiff's assertion, and the concurrent courts rejected the plaintiff's part-performance explanation. The pleading is used for the existence of the alternative account; the adjudicated findings supply the decisive support for the negative premise state.
The Supreme Court expressly identified loan recovery as an available alternative pleading and treated inconsistency with the sale-based claim as immaterial to its permissibility.

The Supreme Court expressly acknowledged that the plaintiff did not make the loan allegation in the plaint. This directly negates actual pleading, without negating the legal possibility of alternative pleading.

The High Court identified the omission as the basis for setting aside the money decree, and the Supreme Court agreed that the loan claim had not been pleaded while rejecting the High Court's ultimate procedural conclusion.

The defendants second party expressly advanced the loan account themselves. The Supreme Court concluded that a claim on that admission could cause no surprise or injustice. Accordingly, the proposition that they lacked a fair opportunity to meet the loan basis is false in the Court's application.

These records establish both components of the defendants' pleaded alternative: their express admission of the loan and their explanation that possession facilitated its interest payment. Their own account directly answered the plaintiff's sale theory.

The trial court made an affirmative finding that the money was advanced as a loan, and the High Court concurred. This is stronger than treating the defendants' pleading as automatically proving the underlying transaction.

F08 supplies the failure of the sale-contract case, while F16 supplies the plaintiff's failure to plead loan recovery. Together they cover the compound premise without treating either component as supplied by mere inference.

The Supreme Court made the no-surprise and no-injustice assessment expressly. The reported Judicial Committee analogy supports the Court's legal reasoning but is not necessary to prove what the target-case defendants pleaded.
The Supreme Court expressly recorded the cessation date as admitted, providing the temporal boundary of the earlier possession period.
gaps: The initial date of possession is not specified.

gaps: Actual transmission and delivery are not established by the supplied reasoning.

all_original_uses.basis: The trial finding establishes the loan character of the Rs. 30,000 advance; the Supreme Court's reasoning supplies its assessment of the defendants' use of the money and the justification for some interest.

The Supreme Court expressly recorded that counsel for both sides left the question of interest to its determination. The Court's subsequent choice of 4% is a legal and discretionary application, not a premise proved from the final order.
