all_opposition.description: The plaintiff's asserted sale consideration and part-performance possession conflict with the defendants second party's loan and interest-facilitation explanation. They concern the same Rs. 30,000 and possession arrangement, not two separate transactions.
all_opposition.resolution: The trial and High Court accepted the loan explanation and rejected proof of the sale-based explanation.

all_opposition.description: The plaintiff attributed notice of the alleged prior sale contract to the later purchasers. The defendants first party denied notice, and both lower courts found that they purchased for value without notice.
all_opposition.resolution: The subsequent purchasers' value-without-notice account was accepted in the factual findings.

all_opposition.description: The High Court treated the absence of a loan prayer as barring the money decree. The Supreme Court distinguished that omission from the defendants' own express admission and absence of prejudice.
all_opposition.resolution: The pleading omission remained a fact, but its supposed absolute consequence was rejected.

all_opposition.description: The Judicial Committee's unpleaded restitution relief in a void-mortgage dispute was cited by analogy to justify non-prejudicial alternative relief. Its mortgage facts, section 65 foundation, and ex parte setting remain confined to that precedent.
all_opposition.resolution: Analogical support for the procedural principle only.

all_opposition.description: The cited Judicial Committee practice admits exceptional departure from concurrent factual findings. Its reported proposition does not establish any exceptional circumstance in the present case.
all_opposition.resolution: The Supreme Court found none in this appeal.

all_opposition.description: The alleged hundi tender and refusal were contested by the plaintiff's denial of receipt. The Supreme Court additionally doubted legal sufficiency even if the alleged events were assumed true.
all_opposition.resolution: The tender defence did not defeat later interest, but the Court did not make a final factual determination of delivery or a conclusive independent tender-validity finding.

all_opposition.description: The defendants pleaded 6% annual loan interest and the trial court initially granted 6% from the suit date. The Supreme Court instead excluded the period of possession and fixed 4% from 1 September 1943.
all_opposition.resolution: The operative post-possession interest measure is the Supreme Court's 4% determination, not the pleaded or original trial-court rate.

all_opposition.description: The source describes the alleged sale arrangement as occurring in late October 1945 but gives 28 October 1941 for payment under it, despite the reported later sale and 1943 lawsuit.
all_opposition.resolution: No correction inferred. The apparent inconsistency is preserved as a limitation of the rendered plaintiff-account chronology.

all_opposition.description: The final refusal of specific performance and limited money award result from factual findings, appellate restraint, procedural fairness, and interest assessment. The operative decree is not used as independent proof of the underlying loan, contract failure, or possession history.
all_opposition.resolution: Reasoning-to-disposition direction preserved.

all_limitations: Only the supplied judgment is used. No external authority, fact checking, prior answer, or other conversation contributes to this reconstruction.
All facts, rules, uses, interpretations and references are unverified model proposals rather than human-validated gold labels.
The frontmatter and headnote are not substituted for the Supreme Court's operative reasoning. The judgment's own reasoning controls where a narrower conclusion is required.

Party pleadings and counsel submissions are preserved as attributed statements. Their mere inclusion does not establish the underlying transaction, notice, payment route, delivery of an instrument, or legal entitlement.
The parties' competing sale-price and loan accounts concern one contested Rs. 30,000 transaction and associated possession arrangement. No second financial or possession event is invented.

all_opposition.description: The Trustees' original lessor position and the 1925 municipal vesting establish the relevant local-authority succession.
Original authority lease, derivative assignment to the Society and monthly occupation by Patel establish the material litigant relationships.

The Court's building-title evaluation depends on the actual bargain, both parts of the demise, reserved controls and legally characterized lease enjoyment, with financing and term considered rather than excluded.

Respondent and High Court interpretations attributed substantial ownership to the lessee; the Supreme Court rejected that characterization using the indenture, contractual controls and enjoyment-versus-title distinction.
Lessee-funded construction and the 999-year term were accepted, but the inference that they transferred building ownership to the lessee was rejected.
The agreement-specific conclusion of local-authority ownership of the building supplies the factual foundation for the section 4(1) premises exemption.
The different wording of section 4(1)'s first and second parts underpins the property-based, rather than relationship-only, scope of the exemption.
The subtenant-protection objection was weighed against the Court's identified public-property purposes and conditional section 15 consequences.
The section 15 hypothetical supports the broad interpretation of the premises exemption but establishes no actual prohibited subletting.
Once the authority-owned premises are found outside the Act, the positive statutory coverage condition for section 28 fails.
Authority to investigate jurisdiction is distinct from the later determination that section 28 does not exclude the City Civil Court in this case.
The Supreme Court reversed the High Court's applicability and jurisdiction conclusions but agreed with its rejection of the preliminary objection to a court assessing its own jurisdiction.
Property ownership, statutory exemption and forum jurisdiction explain the restoration of the trial decree. The arrow is one-way: the final order is not evidence proving those premises.
Patel's payment and compliance claims remain attributed assertions for purposes of the appellate reasoning; no conclusion that they were false follows from the failure of his rent-control defence.

The reported observations on reversionary interests and the ordinary meaning of property or belonging support interpretive analysis. They do not establish the historical title or events of New Sitaram Building.

The suit included possession and mesne-profit claims and the trial issues mentioned compensation, but the supplied appellate reasoning does not independently specify every monetary adjudication or resolve every asserted tenancy-compliance fact.

all_limitations.text: All proposed facts, rules and applications are based exclusively on the supplied judgment identified by turn0file0 and its IK-732701 line markers. No external research, other conversations, prior model reviews or independent case materials were used.

Statements attributed to Patel, his counsel or the Society are preserved as pleadings or arguments. Their accuracy is not presumed. The Supreme Court's separately reasoned findings are distinguished from those statements.

The City Civil Court's decree, the High Court's reversal and the Supreme Court's resolution occupy different procedural levels. The High Court's ownership and coverage holdings are not treated as final controlling legal conclusions.

The procedural description at IK-732701:L119 dates the High Court judgment and order to 12 December 1949, while the Supreme Court narrative at IK-732701:L122 gives 2 December 1949. This internal difference is preserved without external correction. Both passages describe the same intermediate reversal; the source does not establish two distinct appellate decisions.
The supplied rendering contains typographical and transcription irregularities. Short quotations retain source wording. Separate passages are not combined into fabricated continuous quotations.

Only the section 4(1), section 15 and section 28 propositions expressly described or applied in this judgment are reconstructed. The source does not support a complete statement of every provision of the 1947 Act.

Sections 105 and 108 of the Transfer of Property Act are used as characterized by the Supreme Court. No external generalization about fixtures, ownership of every lessee-constructed structure or comparative English and Indian law is supplied.

Clark v. Downes, Rudler v. Franks and Heritable Reversionary Company v. Mullar appear as reported authorities in the judgment. Their general legal observations cannot establish any event, agreement or title concerning the target property.

Contractual rights to forfeit, re-enter, inspect and restrict alterations are recorded as rights or covenants. The supplied judgment does not establish that forfeiture or contractual re-entry actually occurred.

The respondent's direct-landlord limitation, authority-only-beneficiary theory, substantial-lessee-ownership position, deferred-vesting explanation and subtenant-protection argument are substantive contrary material. They are not converted into operative rules accepted by the Supreme Court.

The third part of section 4(1) expressly makes the Act applicable to premises let to Government or a local authority. The actual identified original lease ran from the local authority to a private lessee's receiver. No broader hypothetical determination is inferred.
The final appellate order is recorded as a disposition, never used as the factual premise proving the property's ownership or the Act's nonapplicability.

The supplied appellate reasoning does not separately verify Patel's claimed regular payments or complete tenancy compliance, fully analyze every possible nonstatutory defence, or reproduce any specific monetary calculation. These limits do not negate the restored trial decree.
Where the record does not independently establish a fact, it is treated as unknown or not separately decided. Silence is not converted into proof that the event or entitlement did not exist.

Multiple evidence records are combined for a premise only when the combined records establish its specified actors, property, relationship and material event. An ownership allegation alone does not fill a compound ownership-and-statutory-status premise.

OPEN_TEXT denotes the Court's contextual contractual or purposive legal evaluation. ALL is used only where the expressed rule supports jointly required conditions. No artificial negative alternatives or unstated statutory exceptions are created.

The reconstruction, fact classifications, rule abstractions, use judgments, premise states, target conclusions and relations are unverified model proposals based solely on the supplied judgment, not human-verified gold annotations.

all_original_uses.basis: The original indenture identifies the authority as lessor, and the statutory vesting transfers the Trustees' property to the Municipality. all_opposition.description: The Trustees' original lessor position and the 1925 municipal vesting establish the relevant local-authority succession.
Original authority lease, derivative assignment to the Society and monthly occupation by Patel establish the material litigant relationships.

The Court's building-title evaluation depends on the actual bargain, both parts of the demise, reserved controls and legally characterized lease enjoyment, with financing and term considered rather than excluded.

Respondent and High Court interpretations attributed substantial ownership to the lessee; the Supreme Court rejected that characterization using the indenture, contractual controls and enjoyment-versus-title distinction.
Lessee-funded construction and the 999-year term were accepted, but the inference that they transferred building ownership to the lessee was rejected.
The agreement-specific conclusion of local-authority ownership of the building supplies the factual foundation for the section 4(1) premises exemption.
The different wording of section 4(1)'s first and second parts underpins the property-based, rather than relationship-only, scope of the exemption.
The subtenant-protection objection was weighed against the Court's identified public-property purposes and conditional section 15 consequences.
The section 15 hypothetical supports the broad interpretation of the premises exemption but establishes no actual prohibited subletting.
Once the authority-owned premises are found outside the Act, the positive statutory coverage condition for section 28 fails.
Authority to investigate jurisdiction is distinct from the later determination that section 28 does not exclude the City Civil Court in this case.
The Supreme Court reversed the High Court's applicability and jurisdiction conclusions but agreed with its rejection of the preliminary objection to a court assessing its own jurisdiction.
Property ownership, statutory exemption and forum jurisdiction explain the restoration of the trial decree. The arrow is one-way: the final order is not evidence proving those premises.
Patel's payment and compliance claims remain attributed assertions for purposes of the appellate reasoning; no conclusion that they were false follows from the failure of his rent-control defence.

The reported observations on reversionary interests and the ordinary meaning of property or belonging support interpretive analysis. They do not establish the historical title or events of New Sitaram Building.

The unchanged exception and its expected polarity are not altered.

The adopted statutory construction treats immunity as attaching to qualifying premises and available to a derivative lessee. The competing authority-only interpretation and concern for subtenant protection were considered and rejected as limits on the first part's meaning.
The section 15 subletting discussion is conditional judicial reasoning, not proof that an actual unlawful subletting occurred.

all_opposition.description: The Trustees' original lessor position and the 1925 municipal vesting establish the relevant local-authority succession.
Original authority lease, derivative assignment to the Society and monthly occupation by Patel establish the material litigant relationships.

The Court's building-title evaluation depends on the actual bargain, both parts of the demise, reserved controls and legally characterized lease enjoyment, with financing and term considered rather than excluded.

Respondent and High Court interpretations attributed substantial ownership to the lessee; the Supreme Court rejected that characterization using the indenture, contractual controls and enjoyment-versus-title distinction.
Lessee-funded construction and the 999-year term were accepted, but the inference that they transferred building ownership to the lessee was rejected.
The agreement-specific conclusion of local-authority ownership of the building supplies the factual foundation for the section 4(1) premises exemption.
The different wording of section 4(1)'s first and second parts underpins the property-based, rather than relationship-only, scope of the exemption.
The subtenant-protection objection was weighed against the Court's identified public-property purposes and conditional section 15 consequences.
The section 15 hypothetical supports the broad interpretation of the premises exemption but establishes no actual prohibited subletting.
Once the authority-owned premises are found outside the Act, the positive statutory coverage condition for section 28 fails.
Authority to investigate jurisdiction is distinct from the later determination that section 28 does not exclude the City Civil Court in this case.
The Supreme Court reversed the High Court's applicability and jurisdiction conclusions but agreed with its rejection of the preliminary objection to a court assessing its own jurisdiction.
Property ownership, statutory exemption and forum jurisdiction explain the restoration of the trial decree. The arrow is one-way: the final order is not evidence proving those premises.
Patel's payment and compliance claims remain attributed assertions for purposes of the appellate reasoning; no conclusion that they were false follows from the failure of his rent-control defence.

The reported observations on reversionary interests and the ordinary meaning of property or belonging support interpretive analysis. They do not establish the historical title or events of New Sitaram Building.

The suit included possession and mesne-profit claims and the trial issues mentioned compensation, but the supplied appellate reasoning does not independently specify every monetary adjudication or resolve every asserted tenancy-compliance fact.

all_limitations.text: All proposed facts, rules and applications are based exclusively on the supplied judgment identified by turn0file0 and its IK-732701 line markers. No external research, other conversations, prior model reviews or independent case materials were used.

Statements attributed to Patel, his counsel or the Society are preserved as pleadings or arguments. Their accuracy is not presumed. The Supreme Court's separately reasoned findings are distinguished from those statements.

The City Civil Court's decree, the High Court's reversal and the Supreme Court's resolution occupy different procedural levels. The High Court's ownership and coverage holdings are not treated as final controlling legal conclusions.

The procedural description at IK-732701:L119 dates the High Court judgment and order to 12 December 1949, while the Supreme Court narrative at IK-732701:L122 gives 2 December 1949. This internal difference is preserved without external correction. Both passages describe the same intermediate reversal; the source does not establish two distinct appellate decisions.
The supplied rendering contains typographical and transcription irregularities. Short quotations retain source wording. Separate passages are not combined into fabricated continuous quotations.

Only the section 4(1), section 15 and section 28 propositions expressly described or applied in this judgment are reconstructed. The source does not support a complete statement of every provision of the 1947 Act.

Sections 105 and 108 of the Transfer of Property Act are used as characterized by the Supreme Court. No external generalization about fixtures, ownership of every lessee-constructed structure or comparative English and Indian law is supplied.

Clark v. Downes, Rudler v. Franks and Heritable Reversionary Company v. Mullar appear as reported authorities in the judgment. Their general legal observations cannot establish any event, agreement or title concerning the target property.

all_opposition.explanation: The original immovable-property claim developed into a compromise money decree and its execution. The current contested entitlement concerns procedural restoration of execution rather than the underlying land.
The earlier bona fide assignment finding supports historical standing to execute but does not itself determine ownership or possession of the Howrah property.
The High Court initially required inquiry into hypothetical useful steps. The Supreme Court considered such inquiry unnecessary and insufficient to justify revisional interference.

The post-remand Subordinate Judge considered useful action impossible; the later High Court and Supreme Court narrative contemplated possibilities. These are incompatible evaluations of the same hypothetical situation, not evidence of multiple actual events.
A limitation objection was made and answered in the executing court. Neither record alone establishes a comprehensive Supreme Court rule overriding limitation.

The decree-holder challenged remand jurisdiction, compensatory costs and interest restrictions; the judgment-debtors contested restoration and asserted negligence and accrued protection. The Court decided the case without adjudicating every contention.
Execution-sale decisions were discussed as authorities urged for appealability but were not treated as governing the target collateral restoration order.
The statute and adopted precedents supply the section 115 legal standard. The Supreme Court's separate application supplies the conclusion that no statutory jurisdictional defect occurred here.
The March 1946 reconsideration and February 1947 High Court order followed the initial remand. Their invalidity derives from the independently established jurisdictional defect in that remand.
The substantive procedural and jurisdictional reasoning supports the final disposition. The final disposition is not used as circular proof of its own premises.

all_limitations: This reconstruction uses only the complete judgment rendering supplied with the task. No external case law, searches, other conversations or prior model reviews were used.
All source references identify locations in the supplied rendering; they do not themselves signify judicial approval of a statement.
Statements by counsel, lower-court findings, hypothetical judicial reasoning, reported precedents, adopted Supreme Court findings and operative orders retain distinct statuses.

The judgment rendering contains textual irregularities and apparent transcription errors. The reconstruction preserves material meaning where supported and does not silently supply missing evidence or repair uncertain figures or statutory citations.

The original Howrah immovable property is not identified by parcel, boundaries or other adequate title particulars. Its ownership, possession and tenancy status cannot be reconstructed from the supplied judgment.
The historical assignment issue and past accounting disputes are relevant background but are not interchangeable with the restoration question decided in these appeals.

The competing accounts of what the decree-holder's pleader could have done on 10 March 1945 concern one counterfactual situation. The Court's rejection of the need to decide it does not prove either possible action or impossibility.
The Supreme Court's legal treatment of the original restoration order must not be conflated with the different reasoning and relief entered after the High Court's remand.

Failure to establish a particular entitlement, action or jurisdictional defect is not treated as proof of its factual opposite. Express negative determinations are identified separately from unresolved matters.
The finding that the April 1945 order did not finally determine execution, discharge or satisfaction prevents treating procedural restoration as final proof of the outstanding decretal balance.
The removal of the post-remand interest and compensatory-costs terms is not recast as an independent adjudication of every contractual or decretal financial entitlement.
The reported execution-sale appealability authorities remain distinguished rather than conclusively disapproved on their own facts.
The reported Privy Council decisions supply adopted legal standards but do not establish events occurring in the target execution proceeding.

The reproduced judgment includes a reference to section 116 in its concluding jurisdictional discussion, while the quoted statute, extended analysis and other conclusions concern section 115. This proposal follows the expressly developed section 115 analysis without treating the inconsistent reference as an additional adopted rule.

The operator OPEN_TEXT is used where the Supreme Court's determination depends on judicial evaluation or legal characterization rather than a source-supported mechanical conjunction or disjunction. ALL and ANY are reserved for combinations directly supported by the judgment.

gaps: The pleader's actual hypothetical submission remains unknown, but it is not required for this premise.

gaps: The Supreme Court did not determine the correctness of the reported sale-order decisions.

gaps: A precedent's legal standard does not establish the target case's procedural events.

The final disposition identifies the relief granted but cannot independently prove the jurisdictional invalidity that supplies its premise. That premise is supported instead by F26 and U22.
gaps: Using the final order alone to prove the invalidity of the remand would be circular.

all_opposition.explanation: The original immovable-property claim developed into a compromise money decree and its execution. The current contested entitlement concerns procedural restoration of execution rather than the underlying land.
The earlier bona fide assignment finding supports historical standing to execute but does not itself determine ownership or possession of the Howrah property.
The High Court initially required inquiry into hypothetical useful steps. The Supreme Court considered such inquiry unnecessary and insufficient to justify revisional interference.

The post-remand Subordinate Judge considered useful action impossible; the later High Court and Supreme Court narrative contemplated possibilities. These are incompatible evaluations of the same hypothetical situation, not evidence of multiple actual events.
A limitation objection was made and answered in the executing court. Neither record alone establishes a comprehensive Supreme Court rule overriding limitation.

The decree-holder challenged remand jurisdiction, compensatory costs and interest restrictions; the judgment-debtors contested restoration and asserted negligence and accrued protection. The Court decided the case without adjudicating every contention.
Execution-sale decisions were discussed as authorities urged for appealability but were not treated as governing the target collateral restoration order.
The statute and adopted precedents supply the section 115 legal standard. The Supreme Court's separate application supplies the conclusion that no statutory jurisdictional defect occurred here.
The March 1946 reconsideration and February 1947 High Court order followed the initial remand. Their invalidity derives from the independently established jurisdictional defect in that remand.
The substantive procedural and jurisdictional reasoning supports the final disposition. The final disposition is not used as circular proof of its own premises.

all_opposition.explanation: The original immovable-property claim developed into a compromise money decree and its execution. The current contested entitlement concerns procedural restoration of execution rather than the underlying land.
The earlier bona fide assignment finding supports historical standing to execute but does not itself determine ownership or possession of the Howrah property.
The High Court initially required inquiry into hypothetical useful steps. The Supreme Court considered such inquiry unnecessary and insufficient to justify revisional interference.

The post-remand Subordinate Judge considered useful action impossible; the later High Court and Supreme Court narrative contemplated possibilities. These are incompatible evaluations of the same hypothetical situation, not evidence of multiple actual events.
A limitation objection was made and answered in the executing court. Neither record alone establishes a comprehensive Supreme Court rule overriding limitation.

The decree-holder challenged remand jurisdiction, compensatory costs and interest restrictions; the judgment-debtors contested restoration and asserted negligence and accrued protection. The Court decided the case without adjudicating every contention.
Execution-sale decisions were discussed as authorities urged for appealability but were not treated as governing the target collateral restoration order.
The statute and adopted precedents supply the section 115 legal standard. The Supreme Court's separate application supplies the conclusion that no statutory jurisdictional defect occurred here.
The March 1946 reconsideration and February 1947 High Court order followed the initial remand. Their invalidity derives from the independently established jurisdictional defect in that remand.
The substantive procedural and jurisdictional reasoning supports the final disposition. The final disposition is not used as circular proof of its own premises.

The original Howrah immovable property is not identified by parcel, boundaries or other adequate title particulars. Its ownership, possession and tenancy status cannot be reconstructed from the supplied judgment.
